content: The activity was increased by approximately 45% when compared to 18 patients aged between 18 and 30 years. Clinical study data involving elderly patients (n = 1522) indicate that there were no significant differences in safety profiles between elderly and younger patients. Pharmacokinetic studies with another statin, which shares a similar primary route of elimination, suggest that patients with severe renal insufficiency (as measured by creatinine clearance) may experience higher systemic exposure at a given dose level. Although the exact mechanism remains unclear, cyclosporine has been shown to increase the area under the curve (AUC) of statins. The increase in AUC for simvastatin acid is thought to be partially due to the inhibition of CYP3A4. Elevated plasma levels of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity are associated with an increased risk of myopathy. Inhibitors of CYP3A4 can elevate plasma levels of HMG-CoA reductase inhibitory activity, thereby increasing the risk of myopathy. In a study involving 12 healthy volunteers, simvastatin at an 80-mg dose did not affect the metabolism of the probe CYP3A4 substrates midazolam and erythromycin. This finding indicates that simvastatin is not an inhibitor of CYP3A4 and, therefore, is not expected to influence the plasma levels of other drugs metabolized by CYP3A4. In a 72-week carcinogenicity study, mice were administered daily doses of simvastatin at 25, 100, and 400 mg/kg body weight. These doses resulted in mean plasma drug levels approximately 1, 4, and 8 times higher, respectively, than the mean human plasma drug levels (based on total inhibitory activity measured by AUC) following an 80-mg oral dose. Liver carcinomas were significantly increased in high-dose females and in midand high-dose males, with a maximum incidence of 90% observed in males. The incidence of liver adenomas was significantly elevated in midand high-dose females. Drug treatment also significantly increased the incidence of lung adenomas in midand high-dose males and females. Adenomas of the Harderian gland (a gland of the eye in rodents) were significantly more frequent in high-dose mice compared to controls. No evidence of a tumorigenic effect was observed at a dose of 25 mg/kg/day.
